referenceTopics.title: Know what each language is for
notes: C is commonly used for procedural systems programming. C++ supports procedural, object-oriented and generic styles; it is not simply C with classes. C# is a separate language targeting .NET, with garbage collection.
PHP commonly executes on the server to build responses. HTML/CSS describe browser content/presentation; JavaScript can run in browsers and on servers. Python supports scripts, services and data work.
Name the language and runtime before making a rule about typing, inheritance or memory. PHP supports type declarations even though variables are dynamically typed.

drills.prompt: A PHP page sends HTML to a browser. Where did PHP execute, and what renders the HTML?
drills.answer: PHP usually executes on the server; the browser parses and renders the resulting HTML.

drills.prompt: Correct this claim: C#, C++ and C are just three versions of one language.
drills.answer: They are distinct languages. C++ supports multiple paradigms including OOP and generics; C# commonly targets .NET and has managed memory.
criteria: One meaningful runtime or paradigm distinction

referenceTopics.example: Python runs scripts/services; JavaScript runs in browsers and on servers.
referenceTopics.summary: Separate a language from its runtime and the environment where it executes.

referenceTopics.title: Java runtime and generic types
notes: The JVM executes Java bytecode. A JDK supplies development tools such as javac plus runtime support. JRE is the runtime-environment concept; distribution packaging varies.
Generics parameterize types: List<String> communicates the element type and enables compile-time checks. A generic is not a sorting algorithm.

drills.prompt: You have Java source and need to compile and run it. Distinguish JDK, JVM and JRE.
drills.answer: Use JDK development tools to compile source into bytecode. The JVM executes it; JRE describes runtime libraries and execution support.

drills.prompt: What does List<String> tell a Java caller?
drills.answer: This is a list whose declared element type is String, with compiler checks on compatible use.

referenceTopics.example: List<String> names a list of strings; javac compiles Java source.
referenceTopics.summary: The JVM runs bytecode; the JDK supplies development tools. Generics describe type parameters.

referenceTopics.title: Classes, objects and methods
notes: A class describes a type; an object is an instance. Instantiation creates an instance: Python uses ClassName(...), while Java commonly uses new ClassName(...).
Methods operate through an object or class. Instance state belongs to a particular object; class-level mutable state can accidentally be shared.
The common four OOP teaching concepts are abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Explain a concrete example, not just the list.

drills.prompt: In Python, what is the difference between CounterBox and CounterBox()?
drills.answer: CounterBox names the class. CounterBox() calls it to create an instance, initialized through its constructor machinery.

drills.prompt: Name the four common OOP pillars, then describe one with an example.
drills.answer: Abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. For encapsulation, an account exposes deposit(amount) that validates a positive amount instead of allowing arbitrary balance changes.

referenceTopics.example:
class User: ...
user = User()
# OOP: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism.
referenceTopics.summary: A class defines a type; an object is an instance with its own state and behavior.

referenceTopics.title: Choose a collection
notes: Use a sequence for ordered values, a set for uniqueness/membership, and a dictionary for key/value lookup or counts.
A stack is LIFO; a queue is FIFO. In Python, list append/pop supports a stack; deque append/popleft supports a queue without shifting every remaining element.
A heap supports repeated access to the highest-priority item without fully sorting all values. Python 3.12 heapq is a min-heap.

drills.prompt: Choose structures for undo history, breadth-first traversal and counting repeated names.
drills.answer: Undo history: stack. Breadth-first traversal: queue. Repeated-name counts: dictionary or Counter.

drills.prompt: For values [5, 1, 4] in a Python 3.12 min-heap, which value is popped first? Is the whole heap sorted?
drills.answer: 1 is popped first. A heap is partially ordered, not a fully sorted sequence.

referenceTopics.example: dict: key lookup · set: membership · list: ordered items · deque: queue
referenceTopics.summary: Choose a structure by the operations you need, not by habit.

referenceTopics.title: Git and collaboration
notes: Git tracks repository history locally. GitHub is a hosting/collaboration service. A commit is local until published to a remote.
clone creates a local repository; fetch updates remote-tracking information; pull fetches and integrates using its selected strategy. push publishes refs/commits when authorized.
A branch is a ref within a repository; a fork is a separate hosted repository. Review a diff and tests before proposing a merge.

drills.prompt: You committed locally. Has GitHub changed? What would publish the branch?
drills.answer: A local commit does not update GitHub. An explicitly authorized push publishes the branch to its configured remote.

drills.prompt: Explain fetch versus pull without assuming pull always merges.
drills.answer: Fetch obtains objects and updates remote-tracking refs. Pull also integrates the selected remote branch, using merge or rebase as configured/requested.

referenceTopics.example:
git status → review diff → test → commit
A commit is not automatically published.
referenceTopics.summary: Commit records local history; fetch retrieves remote history; merge/rebase integrates it.

referenceTopics.title: From URL to a rendered page
notes: A browser locates a server, establishes a connection, requests resources and processes responses. HTTPS adds TLS protection. Caches can avoid some network requests.
HTML is parsed into a DOM tree; CSS styles content; JavaScript handles behavior. Not every click needs a new server-rendered page.
The DOM is a document programming interface, not the JavaScript language. <!doctype html> selects standards rendering; it does not validate your markup.

drills.prompt: Explain a page load from request to visible content in three steps.
drills.answer: Request resources from a server (or cache), receive responses, then parse HTML/build DOM and apply CSS/execute JavaScript to render and interact.

drills.prompt: What does <!doctype html> accomplish, and what does it not guarantee?
drills.answer: It selects standards/no-quirks rendering. It does not prove the HTML is valid or guarantee cross-browser perfection.

referenceTopics.example: DNS → connection/TLS → HTTP → HTML/DOM + CSS + JavaScript
referenceTopics.summary: A page load involves finding the server, securing the connection, requesting resources and rendering them.

referenceTopics.title: HTTP requests and responses
notes: GET retrieves a representation with intended read-only semantics. POST asks the target resource to process submitted content. Method semantics do not guarantee secrecy.
200: success; 201: created; 400: bad request; 401: authentication needed/invalid; 403: forbidden; 404: resource not found/disclosed; 405: method not allowed; 500: server error.
Headers, URL and body all carry request information. A POST body is observable to endpoints and potentially logs; protect sensitive traffic with HTTPS and appropriate logging.

drills.prompt: An existing endpoint supports GET, but you send DELETE. What status describes that method mismatch?
drills.answer: 405 Method Not Allowed. The response should identify allowed methods through Allow.
criteria: Method is not allowed on this resource

drills.prompt: Does a POST body make a password secret? Explain.
drills.answer: No. Use HTTPS for transport encryption and avoid leaking sensitive fields in logs. A body is not a security boundary.

referenceTopics.example:
GET /users/7 → 200
POST /users → 201
401: authentication · 403: permission
referenceTopics.summary: HTTP methods express request intent; status codes describe the result. HTTPS protects traffic in transit.

referenceTopics.title: Read and modify relational data
notes: SELECT projects columns; FROM chooses input; WHERE filters rows; INSERT adds rows; UPDATE changes rows; DELETE removes rows. DDL such as CREATE/ALTER/DROP changes schema objects.
Use explicit columns and a deliberate WHERE for modifications. NULL represents missing/unknown data; compare with IS NULL rather than = NULL.
SQL keyword case, identifier case, string comparison and statement terminators are different concerns. PostgreSQL details are examples, not rules for every engine.

drills.prompt: Given employees(name, active), write a query for names where active is the integer 1.
drills.answer: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE active = 1;

drills.prompt: Correct: SQL is never case sensitive, and semicolons are never necessary.
drills.answer: Keywords are generally case insensitive. Identifier quoting and text comparison follow engine/collation rules. Terminators depend on the execution context.

referenceTopics.example:
SELECT name FROM users WHERE active = TRUE;
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL -- not = NULL
referenceTopics.summary: Select the columns and rows you need. Treat missing values explicitly.

referenceTopics.title: Keys and referential integrity
notes: A primary key identifies rows through unique, non-null column values; it can be composite. A foreign key requires a matching referenced key unless its null semantics permit otherwise.
Referenced keys need not be the primary key: eligible unique keys can be referenced. A self-reference can model an employee manager.
Integrity and performance are separate. PostgreSQL creates a primary-key index, but a key does not guarantee every query will be fast.

drills.prompt: orders.customer_id references customers.id. What does the foreign key prevent?
drills.answer: It prevents an order from referencing a non-existent customer key, subject to the constraint/null rules. It is a data-integrity relationship.

drills.prompt: Can a foreign key reference the same table or an eligible unique non-primary key?
drills.answer: Yes to both, where the engine and referenced constraint support it.
criteria: Eligible unique key can be referenced

referenceTopics.example:
orders.customer_id → customers.id
A key can contain more than one column.
referenceTopics.summary: Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys enforce relationships to eligible referenced keys.

referenceTopics.title: Join rows without losing the unmatched ones
notes: INNER retains matches. LEFT retains every left row and matching right rows. RIGHT is the mirrored case. FULL retains matches and unmatched rows from both sides.
An unmatched outer-join side becomes NULL. Two matching right rows produce two joined rows; joins are not simply set-intersection diagrams.
A right-side WHERE filter can remove NULL-padded rows from a LEFT join. Put the condition in ON when you intend to preserve unmatched left rows.

drills.prompt: Customer A has two orders and B has none. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders produce?
drills.answer: Three rows: two for A and one NULL-padded order side for B.

drills.prompt: Write a join returning every customer name and any order ID. Tables: customers(id,name), orders(id,customer_id).
drills.answer: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
criteria: Select customer name and order ID

drills.prompt: What does FULL OUTER JOIN add beyond LEFT JOIN?
drills.answer: It also preserves unmatched right-side rows with a NULL-padded left side.

referenceTopics.example:
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
Filtering o in WHERE may remove unmatched customers.
referenceTopics.summary: INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN also keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs on the right.

referenceTopics.title: Aggregate, group and handle missing values
notes: GROUP BY creates groups for aggregate calculations. WHERE filters input rows; HAVING filters groups. MAX returns the largest non-null value in a group.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values. In a LEFT join, count the child key to avoid counting a NULL-padded row as a child.

drills.prompt: Write department maximum salary from employees(department,salary), keeping groups whose max exceeds 100000.
drills.answer: SELECT department, MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING MAX(salary) > 100000;

drills.prompt: After customers LEFT JOIN orders, why might COUNT(*) incorrectly report one order for a customer with none?
drills.answer: The outer join still produces one padded row. COUNT(o.id) counts only non-null matching order IDs.

referenceTopics.example:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
referenceTopics.summary: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups afterward.

referenceTopics.title: React, JSX, forms and CSS
notes: React components describe UI. JSX is syntax transformed into JavaScript; braces embed JavaScript expressions. JSON exchanges data; it is not JSX.
State changes schedule UI updates. Form UI, state handling and validation are different responsibilities. Yup supplies schema parsing/validation, not form widgets.
A CSS class is reusable across elements. An HTML id should be unique in the document. Flexbox lays out one main axis at a time; grid supports two-dimensional layouts.

drills.prompt: An API returns JSON, and a React component uses JSX. Explain the difference.
drills.answer: JSON represents data. JSX expresses UI markup inside JavaScript and is transformed before execution.

drills.prompt: You need a form and field validation. Does adding Yup create the form UI?
drills.answer: No. Build the form UI/state handling, and use Yup if schema validation fits the requirements.

drills.prompt: Which CSS selector is reusable: .notice or #notice? How would you align a row of buttons?
drills.answer: .notice is a reusable class; #notice identifies an element with that id. A flex container can align a row with gap and align-items.

referenceTopics.summary: Components describe UI; state drives updates. Keep rendering, validation and network behavior distinct.

referenceTopics.title: Abstraction and encapsulation in practice
notes: Abstraction exposes an understandable contract while hiding irrelevant details. Encapsulation controls how state can be accessed/changed and protects invariants.
A deposit(amount) operation can reject a negative amount. An unrestricted setBalance(value) can bypass the same invariant even though it is a setter.
Composition supplies collaborators; inheritance creates a subtype relationship. Prefer a relationship that matches the contract you need rather than inheriting solely for code reuse.

drills.prompt: A class has private balance and setBalance(any_number). Is encapsulation automatically good?
drills.answer: No. Private storage plus an unrestricted setter may still violate invariants. Expose validated operations such as deposit(positive_amount).

drills.prompt: Distinguish abstraction from encapsulation using a payment service.
drills.answer: Abstraction offers charge(amount) without revealing provider details. Encapsulation controls internal credentials/state and validates transitions.

referenceTopics.example:
account.deposit(10) can validate the amount.
A public balance setter could bypass that rule.
referenceTopics.summary: Abstraction exposes a useful contract; encapsulation protects state and invariants.

referenceTopics.title: Polymorphism, overloading and overriding
notes: Polymorphism lets callers use a shared contract with different implementations. For example, several storage adapters can implement save(record).
Java overloading uses different parameter signatures under the same name. Overriding supplies a subtype implementation of an inherited instance method with compatible signature and return rules.
Return type alone cannot distinguish Java overloads. Python does not implement Java-style runtime overloads by repeating def with the same name; the later definition replaces the earlier binding.

drills.prompt: In Java, are calculate(int) and calculate(double) overriding or overloading? What about a child replacing calculate(int)?
drills.answer: Different parameter signatures are overloads. A compatible child implementation of the inherited instance method is an override.

drills.prompt: Can a Java override freely change its parameter types? Can an overload differ only in return type?
drills.answer: No to both. Overriding preserves the relevant signature; Java permits covariant reference returns. Overloading requires distinct signatures.

referenceTopics.example:
storage.save(record) works with different adapters.
Java overloads differ in parameters, not return type alone.
referenceTopics.summary: A shared contract can have several implementations. Overloading and overriding have language-specific rules.

referenceTopics.title: Interfaces and abstract classes: Java scope
notes: A Java abstract class can share instance state and implementations but cannot be directly instantiated. It can be abstract even without abstract methods.
A modern Java interface defines a contract and can also have default, static and private methods plus constants. It has no instance fields.
A Java class has one direct class superclass and can implement multiple interfaces. This is not universal across languages; Python permits multiple class bases.

drills.prompt: Correct: Java interfaces contain only public abstract methods and cannot contain implementations.
drills.answer: They may include default/static implementations and private helper methods. They lack per-instance fields, but may declare constants.

drills.prompt: You need shared per-instance state plus a partial implementation in Java. Which construct fits, and can you instantiate it directly?
drills.answer: An abstract base class can provide that state/implementation. Instantiate a concrete subclass, not the abstract class directly.

referenceTopics.example:
Java: one direct class superclass, multiple interfaces.
Python permits multiple class bases.
referenceTopics.summary: An interface specifies a contract; an abstract class can also share instance state and implementation.

referenceTopics.title: Agile and Scrum without the slogans
notes: Agile emphasizes working software, collaboration, adaptation and feedback. It is not a prescribed sequential checklist and does not require Scrum.
Scrum uses fixed-length Sprints of one month or less. Planning sets the Sprint Goal; Daily Scrum inspects progress; Review inspects outcomes; Retrospective improves how the team works.
Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers have distinct accountabilities. The Daily Scrum is not primarily a manager status report. An increment must meet the Definition of Done.

drills.prompt: Does every Agile team have Sprints? Give the distinction.
drills.answer: No. Agile is a set of values/principles. Scrum is a specific framework that uses Sprints.

drills.prompt: Distinguish a Sprint Review from a Retrospective.
drills.answer: Review inspects the product outcome with stakeholders and adapts future work; Retrospective improves the team’s ways of working.

referenceTopics.example:
Review: inspect the product.
Retrospective: improve how the team works.
referenceTopics.summary: Work in small increments, inspect outcomes and adapt. Scrum is one framework, not a synonym for Agile.

referenceTopics.title: Insertion and bubble sort
notes: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting the next value. Typical stable array insertion sort uses O(n²) worst-case time and O(1) extra storage; already-sorted input can be O(n).
Ordinary bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order values and settles an extreme at one end per pass. With an early-exit flag its best case is O(n), but its worst case remains O(n²).
For nearly sorted data, insertion sort is usually the stronger teaching/default choice between these two. Do not choose an algorithm only from its best-case bound.

drills.prompt: After inserting 2 into the sorted prefix [1,4] of [1,4,2,3], show the array.
drills.answer: [1,2,4,3]. The sorted prefix is now [1,2,4].

drills.prompt: Why does bubble sort remain a weak default even if early exit makes sorted input linear?
drills.answer: Many inputs still require quadratic comparisons/swaps; insertion sort generally handles small/nearly-sorted data more effectively. Best case does not describe every workload.

referenceTopics.example:
Typical array implementations: O(n²) worst-case time.
An early-exit implementation can improve best-case behavior.
referenceTopics.summary: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions.

referenceTopics.title: Merge sort and quicksort
notes: Typical array merge sort divides, sorts and merges. It guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time and usually needs O(n) auxiliary storage; stable merging preserves equal-key order.

Quicksort partitions around a pivot. Randomized/ordinary average analysis gives O(n log n), but very unbalanced partitions can produce O(n²). Recursion space depends on partition balance and implementation.
Median-of-three is a pivot heuristic, not a universal worst-case guarantee. State the implementation before calling a sort stable or in-place.

drills.prompt: Choose between ordinary array merge sort and quicksort when guaranteed O(n log n) time matters. State a tradeoff.
drills.answer: Merge sort gives the worst-case bound, usually with O(n) auxiliary storage. Ordinary quicksort has quadratic worst cases.

drills.prompt: Does median-of-three make ordinary quicksort immune to quadratic behavior?
drills.answer: No. It can improve pivot choice in practice, but does not guarantee balanced partitions for every input.

referenceTopics.example:
Merge sort: O(n log n) typical/worst time.
Quicksort: average O(n log n), worst O(n²).
referenceTopics.summary: Merge sort combines sorted pieces; quicksort partitions around a pivot.

referenceTopics.title: Binary heaps and heapsort
notes: A binary heap is a complete binary tree represented conveniently as an array. In a max-heap each parent is at least its children; siblings and distant nodes need not be ordered.
Bottom-up heap construction is O(n). Sift-down at a node is O(log n) assuming its child subtrees already satisfy the heap property.
Heapsort swaps the max root with the end of the active heap and repairs the reduced heap. It gives O(n log n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary array storage; ordinary heapsort is not stable.

drills.prompt: Is [9,7,8,1,2] a valid max-heap despite 7 coming before 8?
drills.answer: Yes. Each parent is at least its children; heap order does not require siblings or the entire array to be sorted.

drills.prompt: State bottom-up heap-build time, one sift-down time and heapsort worst-case time.
drills.answer: O(n), O(log n), O(n log n), respectively.

referenceTopics.example:
heapq.heappush(heap, value)
smallest = heapq.heappop(heap) # Python 3.12 min-heap
referenceTopics.summary: A heap gives efficient repeated access to the highest-priority item; it is not a fully sorted sequence.

referenceTopics.title: SOLID as design reasoning
notes: S: group responsibilities that change for the same reason. O: provide extension points for expected variation. Neither principle requires a separate class for every line.
L: subtypes preserve the promises of the base contract. I: expose focused interfaces so clients need not depend on unrelated operations.
D: high-level policy and low-level details depend on abstractions. This is Dependency Inversion. Apply it where change/testing justify the indirection.

drills.prompt: Expand SOLID, especially D, then give a small dependency example.
drills.answer: Single Responsibility; Open/Closed; Liskov Substitution; Interface Segregation; Dependency Inversion. A report service depends on a storage contract rather than constructing a specific database client.

drills.prompt: A subtype keeps every method name but throws unsupported errors for valid parent operations. Does that establish Liskov substitution?
drills.answer: No. Clients relying on the base behavior can break. Substitution is about behavior/contracts, not method-name count.

referenceTopics.example:
S: Single Responsibility · O: Open/Closed
L: Liskov Substitution · I: Interface Segregation
D: Dependency Inversion
referenceTopics.summary: SOLID helps reason about responsibilities, contracts and dependency direction.

referenceTopics.title: Inject collaborators and control coupling
notes: Dependency injection means providing a collaborator externally. Constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit; method or property injection can fit other lifetimes/frameworks.
The composition boundary still creates objects, possibly with new. The goal is to move concrete wiring away from business policy, not ban object creation.
A fake storage adapter lets a test exercise report generation without a live database. Too many dependencies can signal too many responsibilities.

drills.prompt: Refactor ReportService creating its own DatabaseClient into a DI design. A short Python sketch is enough.
Is Dependency Injection identical to Dependency Inversion? Must DI remove every new expression?
drills.answer: No. Inversion is a principle about dependency direction/abstractions; injection supplies dependencies. Objects still have to be constructed.

referenceTopics.example:
ReportService(storage)
Tests can supply a fake storage implementation.
referenceTopics.summary: Inject a dependency instead of constructing it inside the code that uses it.

referenceTopics.title: Model data and query performance
notes: Normalization uses dependencies to separate facts and reduce update anomalies. Intentional denormalization can trade more complex writes for faster reads; measure and keep a consistency plan.

Relational and NoSQL systems both have schemas and constraints in practice. Choose based on access patterns, integrity, transactions, scale and operational needs rather than SQL versus unstructured slogans.
Indexes cost storage and write maintenance. Inspect a query plan and actual workload before adding one. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query; use it carefully with mutations.
Clustering can mean physical row organization, a group of servers, or statistical grouping. Clarify which. PostgreSQL CLUSTER reorders a table once and does not keep that ordering automatically.
Transactions group changes into an all-or-nothing unit; concurrency/isolation still needs deliberate design. This extends the source notes into practical architecture reasoning.

drills.prompt: Every order repeats customer_email. What anomaly can occur, and how can normalization help?
drills.answer: Updating only some orders produces inconsistent customer facts. Store customer data once and reference the customer key; still consider historical snapshot requirements.

drills.prompt: A query is slow. Why not add an index on every column?
drills.answer: Indexes use space and slow writes. Inspect filters, joins, selectivity and the plan, then measure a suitable index against the workload.

drills.prompt: Two account updates must succeed together. Which concept helps, and what should you clarify when someone says database clustering?
drills.answer: Use a transaction for atomic updates. Ask whether clustering means physical organization, server topology or statistical grouping.

referenceTopics.example:
Inspect the query plan before adding an index.
Transactions group changes; isolation controls interactions.
referenceTopics.summary: Model relationships and access patterns. Indexes help selected reads but cost storage and write work.

referenceTopics.title: API security and repeatable requests
notes: Prevent SQL injection by binding values with parameterized statements; do not concatenate untrusted input into SQL. Dynamically chosen table/column names need allowlisting or supported identifier composition.
Authentication identifies the caller; authorization checks that caller’s permitted action on a particular resource. Validate inputs server-side and minimize sensitive logging.

Safe methods request read-only behavior. Idempotent methods have the same intended effect when repeated; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics, while POST is not inherently so. Response codes may differ across repeats.

drills.prompt: A login query concatenates a username into SQL. Describe the fix and why escaping alone is a weak default.
drills.answer: Use parameter binding so input is treated as data, not executable SQL syntax. Validate inputs too, but do not replace binding with ad hoc escaping.

drills.prompt: A user is logged in and requests another user’s private record. Which check is missing?
drills.answer: Resource-level authorization. Authentication alone does not grant permission to access every object.

drills.prompt: Can DELETE remain idempotent if the first response is 204 and the second is 404?
drills.answer: Yes. Idempotence concerns the intended server-side effect, not identical response status. The resource remains deleted.

referenceTopics.example:
WHERE email = ? -- parameter bound separately
Never trust a hidden UI button as an access-control boundary.
referenceTopics.summary: Authenticate identity, authorize each operation, validate input and parameterize SQL.

referenceTopics.title: REST, SOAP and the web contract
notes: REST is an architectural style with client/server separation, stateless requests, caching constraints, a uniform interface and layers (optional code on demand). JSON over HTTP alone does not prove REST compliance.
SOAP defines an XML envelope/messaging framework with transport bindings, commonly HTTP. It does not inherently force a stateful session or HTML messages.
For an HTTP resource API, define representations, methods, status codes, validation, pagination, permissions and error behavior. Stateless requests do not mean the database stores no state.

drills.prompt: Correct: SOAP is always stateful, REST is always faster, and SOAP sends HTML.
drills.answer: SOAP uses XML envelopes and does not inherently require sessions. REST is a style; performance depends on workload, protocol use and implementation. HTML is not the SOAP envelope format.

drills.prompt: Design a short contract for creating an order and later fetching it.
drills.answer: POST /orders with validated input; return 201 plus a resource location/representation on creation. GET /orders/{id} reads it. Check caller permissions and define errors.

referenceTopics.example:
PUT /users/7 repeats the intended replacement effect.
A retryable POST may need an idempotency key.
referenceTopics.summary: Define resources, methods, validation, permissions, pagination and predictable errors.

referenceTopics.title: Turn source coding notes into Blind 75 preparation
notes: First clarify output meaning and edge cases. Frequency maps solve counting/mode/anagram checks; sets handle membership; two pointers handle ordered scans; a queue supports breadth-first traversal.

Use the fixed Blind 75 path for full coding practice. Historical non-Blind-75 links are source context, not additions to the required problem inventory. Old COMPLETED labels do not imply current recall.
For a maximum number of disjoint teams needing one p,c,m,b,z each, the bottleneck is the minimum of their counts. Distinguish maximum simultaneous teams from counting every possible combination.
The source’s second team input includes o and cannot support its stated answer of 3. Reject invalid symbols under the stated contract. A corrected valid example bbbbcccmmmmppppzzzz yields 3.

drills.prompt: Given [1,4,8,2,1,7,4,1], return the most frequent value, not the numerically largest duplicate. Explain the approach.
drills.answer: 1 occurs three times. Count values using a dictionary/Counter, then select the maximum count; define tie behavior before coding.

drills.prompt: For pcmbzpcmbz, find the maximum number of disjoint teams needing one of each letter. Why minimum count?
drills.answer: 2. Every team consumes one of each required skill, so the least available skill limits the number; pairing arbitrary members constructs that many teams.

drills.prompt: The source says mppzombpzcmpmzz yields three teams. What must be corrected before implementing?
drills.answer: It contains invalid o and only one c and b. Reject it under the specified alphabet. If explicitly ignoring invalid symbols, the minimum required count is 1; the separate valid sorted example yields 3.

referenceTopics.example:
Contiguous range → consider sliding window.
Sorted search space → consider binary search.
referenceTopics.summary: Recognize the constraint and invariant before choosing a code template.

referenceTopics.title: Explain a solution and its boundaries
notes: For an engineering interview, state inputs/outputs, an invariant, data structure, time/space and at least one boundary case. A passing sample is not proof of correctness.
Fibonacci: define F0=0,F1=1, then reuse earlier states instead of exponential repeated recursion. For primes below N, the sieve marks composite multiples; test N<=2.

For duplicate item records, clarify whether you count extra occurrences or every matching pair, and which attributes define identity. For matrices, distinguish unique-row storage from repeated shared references.

drills.prompt: Two Sum: what invariant does a seen-value map maintain, and what complexity do you expect?
drills.answer: The map contains values/indices processed before the current index. Look up target-current before storing the current item to avoid reusing it; expected O(n) time and O(n) space with ordinary hash behavior.

drills.prompt: How do you improve naive repeated-recursion Fibonacci, and which base convention should you state?
drills.answer: Memoize subproblems or keep the previous two values iteratively. State F0=0 and F1=1; iterative computation uses O(n) time/O(1) auxiliary space under the usual unit-cost arithmetic model.

drills.prompt: A list contains the same item three times. How many duplicates are there?
drills.answer: Clarify the definition: two extra occurrences beyond the first, or three unordered equal pairs. Both are plausible; agree on the contract first.

referenceTopics.example:
What stays true each iteration?
What happens for empty input, duplicates and boundaries?
referenceTopics.summary: Explain the approach, invariant, edge cases and complexity; trace a small input.

referenceTopics.title: Explain a small system for a customer
notes: Start with users, core operations, data sensitivity, scale and reliability needs. Trace browser → API → data store, then discuss one failure path and one measurable tradeoff. This is an application exercise extending the source material.
MVC separates model/data-domain behavior, view/presentation and controller/input coordination. Frameworks apply these boundaries differently.

A dynamic address is typically leased by DHCP and may remain the same for long periods. Static configuration or a reservation provides predictable addressing; dynamic does not mean every request gets a new IP.

drills.prompt: Explain a small reporting web app to a non-specialist, including one failure case and one tradeoff.
drills.answer: The browser asks an API for a report; the API checks permission, reads data and returns a result. Show a clear retry/error state on failure. A cached report can be faster but may be stale.

drills.prompt: Does a DHCP client necessarily change IP on every connection or request? Distinguish static addressing.
drills.answer: No. DHCP leases can be renewed with the same address. Static configuration or a reservation is used when predictable assignment is needed.

referenceTopics.example:
Browser → authenticated API → database
What happens when the database is slow or unavailable?
referenceTopics.summary: Start with requirements, follow the request/data flow, then explain failures and tradeoffs.

referenceTopics.title: Tell a truthful project and teamwork story
notes: Use a short situation → task → your action → result → lesson outline. Explain what you personally did and what evidence supports the result; do not invent metrics or borrow somebody else’s outcome.

Prepare distinct examples for learning something unfamiliar, a technical setback, collaboration/conflict, leadership, failure and a meaningful achievement. Historical source stories are private prompts, not verified scripts.

Describe constraints professionally. Explain your response, tradeoff and learning instead of blaming teammates or making unverifiable accusations. Update career stage and current experience before rehearsing.

drills.prompt: Write a five-line outline for a real project challenge. Use placeholders for facts you still need to verify.
drills.answer: Situation: [context]. Task: [responsibility]. Action: [your specific choices]. Result: [verifiable outcome]. Lesson: [what changed in your approach].

drills.prompt: Your failure answer is only “I persevere.” What is missing?
drills.answer: A specific failure, your responsibility, what you changed, and evidence of a later improvement. A slogan alone does not demonstrate behavior.

drills.prompt: Outline a respectful conflict answer without criticizing a teammate.
drills.answer: Explain the shared goal, the differing views, how you listened/clarified constraints, the agreed action and the observed result. Own your contribution.

referenceTopics.example:
Situation → task → action → result
Distinguish personal work from team outcomes.
referenceTopics.summary: Explain a specific problem, your contribution, evidence of the outcome and what you learned.

referenceTopics.title: Motivation, role fit and questions to ask
notes: For “why this company,” connect verified current work to your relevant experience and the contribution you want to make. Replace dated company claims and vague “nothing to lose” wording with a concrete fit.

State Python experience honestly: distinguish what you can read, build independently, explain with help and are still practicing. For engineering emphasize implementation; for solutions architecture emphasize customer needs and tradeoffs while keeping technical depth.

Useful questions cover actual projects, onboarding, success measures, collaboration, technical ownership, SQL/data expectations, customer feedback and growth. Historical hiring anecdotes are not promises about the next interview.

drills.prompt: Draft a brief motivation answer without inventing company facts or claiming experience you do not have.
drills.answer: I am interested in [verified work/problem] because [real connection]. I have worked on [truthful relevant example], and want to contribute [specific value] while developing [skill].

drills.prompt: Choose three useful questions to ask about either an engineering or solutions architect role.
drills.answer: What would I own in the first three months? How is success measured? How do engineers/architects clarify customer requirements and review tradeoffs?

drills.prompt: How would you describe early Python experience honestly in an interview?
drills.answer: I am building fluency through scripts and algorithm exercises. I can demonstrate [specific verified task] independently; I am still practicing [specific area]. Then show or explain actual code.

referenceTopics.example:
How are releases tested?
How does the team investigate production incidents?
referenceTopics.summary: Connect your experience to the role and ask how the team builds and operates software.

referenceTopics.title: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests
referenceTopics.summary: Test behavior at the smallest useful boundary, then cover important connections and user journeys.
referenceTopics.example:
Unit: price calculation
Integration: repository + database
E2E: browser completes a workflow
notes: Include failure paths, boundaries and alternate valid inputs. A passing suite proves its assertions for the tested cases, not the absence of defects.
Mock external boundaries deliberately; too much mocking can hide integration failures.

referenceTopics.title: Debug a production issue
referenceTopics.summary: Reproduce or characterize the failure, narrow its scope, test a hypothesis and verify the fix.
referenceTopics.example:
Symptoms → logs/request ID → smallest reproduction
→ root cause → regression test → monitored rollout
notes: Avoid recording credentials or sensitive payloads in diagnostic logs. Distinguish the root cause from a workaround.
Change one relevant variable at a time; use measurements rather than guessing where time is spent.

referenceTopics.title: Write understandable functions
referenceTopics.summary: Use specific names, cohesive responsibilities and explicit inputs/outputs. Keep error behavior deliberate.
referenceTopics.example:
parse_user_input(text)
validate_user(user)
save_user(user)
notes: Separate pure transformations from I/O where useful. Avoid both giant functions and needless layers.
Explain why an abstraction helps this codebase; do not apply a design principle as an automatic rule.

referenceTopics.title: Caching and stale data
referenceTopics.summary: Reuse a previous result to reduce repeated work; decide how stale it may be and how it expires.
referenceTopics.example:
Read cache → miss → read database → cache result
TTL bounds freshness; invalidation handles changes.
notes: Consider keys, eviction, invalidation, cache misses and sensitive-data scope. A cache should not accidentally share one user’s result with another.
A cache outage or synchronized expiry can push traffic back onto the database.

referenceTopics.title: Queues, retries and idempotency
referenceTopics.summary: A queue decouples request handling from background work. Plan for duplicates and failures.
referenceTopics.example:
API → queue → worker → saved result
Job ID + idempotent write makes retries safer.
notes: At-least-once delivery can repeat work. Bound retry attempts, use backoff where appropriate and inspect failed jobs.
A queue helps absorb bursts; it does not make slow work disappear or guarantee exactly-once effects.

referenceTopics.title: Load balancing and availability
referenceTopics.summary: Distribute traffic across healthy instances and identify the dependencies that still limit availability.
referenceTopics.example:
Load balancer → stateless application replicas → database
Health checks route around unhealthy replicas.
notes: Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling adds resources to an instance. Both have costs and limits.
Consider state/session handling, database capacity, timeouts, backups and tested recovery. Replicas alone do not guarantee reliability.

referenceTopics.title: Race conditions and atomic changes
referenceTopics.summary: Concurrent requests can read the same old state and overwrite each other. Protect the whole operation.
referenceTopics.example:
Two buyers see stock = 1.
Use an atomic conditional update or an appropriate transaction.
notes: Transactions provide atomic grouping, but isolation and locking choices still matter. Read-modify-write in application code is not automatically atomic.
Consider contention, deadlocks and retry behavior. Explain the database’s guarantees rather than assuming them.

httpCodes: Request refused; permission may be insufficient
Valid syntax, instructions cannot be processed
corrections: SQL keywords are generally case insensitive. Quoted identifiers, text comparisons and collations have engine-specific rules. Statement terminators depend on the client/context.
A primary key enforces uniqueness and non-nullness, not universal query speed. Foreign keys may reference eligible unique keys, including in the same table.
FULL OUTER JOIN retains matched rows and unmatched rows from both sides, padding missing values with NULL. Multiple matches can multiply rows.
D means Dependency Inversion. Dependency injection is a technique that can support it, not the name of the principle.
Preserve the behavioral contract of the base type. Merely keeping method names or adding features does not establish substitutability.
Modern Java interfaces can declare default, static and private methods plus constants. They have no per-instance fields. Abstraction percentages are not a useful rule.
One class superclass is a Java rule, not a universal OOP rule. Python supports multiple class inheritance.
In Java, overriding preserves the method signature and permits a covariant reference return. It does not permit arbitrary parameter-type changes. Return type alone cannot overload a method.
Controlled access and invariant preservation matter; adding unrestricted getters/setters alone does not protect state.
Supply collaborators externally. Constructor injection is often useful, but not the only form. Object creation with new still happens at a composition boundary.
Agile does not require Sprints. Scrum has Sprints of one month or less, an explicit Sprint Goal, Review and Retrospective; it does not guarantee faster delivery.
Git is the version-control system. GitHub hosts repositories and collaboration. Pull fetches and then integrates according to options/configuration, potentially by rebase.
PHP is dynamically typed and supports parameter, return and property declarations; coercion and strict_types affect scalar calls. Type declarations are not universally absent.
Yup validates/parses schemas; it does not create form UI. JSON is a data format. JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension for UI markup, not the usual REST data format.
Safe means intended read-only semantics, not zero logging or security. POST is not inherently secret and need not always mutate data; HTTPS protects either method in transit.
405 means Method Not Allowed, not Method Not Found. A 404 can also intentionally conceal a resource; it is not always a malformed URL.
The HTML doctype selects standards/no-quirks rendering. It does not validate the page or guarantee future compatibility.
SOAP is an XML messaging protocol with transport bindings; REST is an architectural style. SOAP does not inherently require sessions, and neither label guarantees scalability.
Clarify the context: indexed physical row ordering, multiple database servers, and statistical clustering are distinct meanings. PostgreSQL CLUSTER is a one-time table reordering.

A binary heap is complete and partially ordered, with non-strict parent inequalities. Sift-down assumes child subtrees are heaps, not sorted arrays. Ordinary bubble sort settles one end per pass; it is rarely the preferred nearly-sorted choice.
